The energy here at Interlagos is palpable; fireworks light up the sky above the garages, a true carnival atmosphere before the race even begins.
Looking out over the circuit, you can see the favelas nestled in the hills surrounding Interlagos, a stark reminder of the contrast within Brazil.
The sun beats down on the asphalt, the heat radiating off the track as the cars are prepped for a grueling race.
The smell of burning rubber and high-octane fuel hangs heavy in the air; Interlagos is alive and ready to host another chapter in Formula 1 history.
Flags wave frantically in the grandstands, a kaleidoscope of color as the drivers prepare for the formation lap.
The altitude here at Interlagos always adds a unique challenge, impacting the engine performance and putting the drivers under immense physical strain.
The passion of the Brazilian fans is unmatched, their enthusiasm echoing through the valley that cradles this historic circuit.
The atmosphere is electric, a vibrant celebration of motorsport as the drivers navigate the final corner before lining up on the grid.

historicalReferences: Senna's emotional victory in 1991, wrestling with a gearbox stuck in sixth gear, remains one of the most iconic moments in Formula 1 history, right here at Interlagos.
Who can forget Fisichella's controversial win in 2003, awarded days later after a red flag and confusion over the race distance?
Lewis Hamilton’s last-corner overtake on Timo Glock in 2008, snatching the World Championship in the most dramatic fashion, is etched in Interlagos folklore.
The 2012 race saw a chaotic mix of rain and safety cars, ultimately crowning Sebastian Vettel as champion after a nail-biting finish.
Alain Prost's final Grand Prix victory came here in 1993, a fitting end to a legendary career.
Michael Schumacher’s emotional farewell in 2006, battling back after an early puncture, showcased his relentless spirit.
Rubens Barrichello's home race struggles are well-documented, the weight of expectation often proving too much to bear.
Kimi Räikkönen secured his World Championship title here in 2007, a race filled with strategic gambles and on-track drama.
The numerous safety car periods in the 2003 race contributed to the confusion that surrounded Fisichella's victory.
Interlagos has been a stage for countless title deciders, solidifying its place as a truly iconic circuit on the Formula 1 calendar.
cornerCallouts: Drivers will be pushing hard through the Senna S, trying to carry as much speed as possible onto the back straight.
Turn 4, the Descida do Lago, is a critical braking zone, demanding precision and control.
The Ferradura, or Horseshoe, is a long, sweeping corner that tests the car's balance and the driver's nerve.
A good exit from Junção is crucial for setting up a strong run down the main straight.
Turn 12, the Arquibancada, is a fast right-hander where drivers can easily run wide if they're not careful.
The Bico de Pato is a tricky corner, requiring a delicate touch on the throttle to avoid losing time.
The braking zone for Turn 1, the Senna 'S', is notoriously bumpy; drivers will need to be precise to avoid locking up.
That long left-hander at Pinheirinho really puts the lateral G-forces on the drivers. A real test of endurance.
strategyPoints: Tire degradation will be a major factor on this abrasive Interlagos surface, especially with the high temperatures expected today.
The relatively short pit lane here means that pit stops are less costly in terms of time, potentially opening up strategic options.
Fuel consumption will be a concern on this 4.309km circuit, requiring careful management throughout the race.
With multiple overtaking opportunities, expect teams to be aggressive with their strategies to gain track position.
A well-timed safety car period could completely reshuffle the order, making strategic flexibility key.
The elevation changes and high-speed corners put immense stress on the tires, demanding a well-balanced car and a strategic approach to tire management.
The pit window is likely to open relatively early, as teams look to avoid getting caught out by potential safety cars.
Running a longer first stint could pay dividends if a safety car falls at the right moment, but it's a risky gamble on this high-degradation track.
weatherCommentary: The weather in São Paulo is notoriously unpredictable; rain can arrive suddenly and dramatically change the complexion of the race.
Dark clouds are gathering over the circuit; rain could be a factor at any moment.
The humidity is incredibly high today, adding to the already intense physical challenge for the drivers.
The wind direction can change dramatically throughout the day, affecting the car's balance and aerodynamic performance.
The sun is beating down relentlessly, baking the track and increasing tire temperatures.
gridWalkQuotes: "The key to a good result here is managing the tires," says Max Verstappen, "This track is brutal on the rubber."
"Interlagos is a special place," notes Lewis Hamilton, "The energy from the fans is incredible, and it always pushes you to give your all."
"We've worked hard on our race pace," Carlos Sainz Jr. tells us, "Hopefully, we can challenge for a podium today."
"The altitude definitely makes a difference," Charles Leclerc explains, "You can feel the power loss, and it affects the braking points."
"Overtaking here is possible," says George Russell, "But you need to be brave and make the most of every opportunity."
"We're expecting a tough race," Fernando Alonso admits, "Tire management will be crucial, and we need to be ready for anything."
"The key is to stay out of trouble," Lando Norris tells us, "There's always drama here at Interlagos."
"We've got a few strategy options open," Sergio Perez reveals, "We'll see how the race unfolds and react accordingly."
